body.text: Universal Medicine outcast reveals leader Serge Benhayon's predatory tricks
For the first time, a devotee of Australia's biggest cult export has broken its 27-year code of silence.
One night in Australia's New Age capital of northern New South Wales, Lismore tradie Brendan Jones found himself undergoing an exorcism — over the telephone.
On the other end of the line was enigmatic cult leader Serge Benhayon, whose teachings had dictated Brendan's life for decades.
Brendan was in hot water. He'd gone behind Serge's back to have dinner with a friend who'd been excommunicated from their cult, Universal Medicine. And he'd been dobbed in by his own wife.
Brendan hadn't set out to betray his leader. He'd just wanted to understand how his banished friend had gone from Serge's inner circle to being vilified as someone possessed by evil energy.
And he was struck by what their secret reunion showed him. The shunned follower "looked 10 years younger".
"He was joyful," Brendan recalls. "We had a lot of fun."

So much fun, that when Brendan returned from the dinner, his wife was alarmed. A fellow devotee of Universal Medicine, she became convinced that Brendan had been infected by evil energy over his friend's homemade grilled salmon.
This was the kind of spiritual emergency that followers were expected to report. And so despite Brendan pleading not to, she picked up the phone to cult leader Serge.
Soon Brendan found himself clutching the receiver as the guru told him he had been infected with bad energy.
"He basically took it out of me," Brendan says, summarising the phone-line exorcism.
Brendan "didn't understand what the hell was going on" but by the end of Serge's purge, he "felt different".
The cult leader may have used hypnosis, one of the techniques that has led some followers to believe he has "supernatural" powers.

Whatever the case, it was enough to convince Brendan to turn his back on his shunned friend and any thoughts he'd planted about life beyond the insular cult, which controls everything from devotees' diets to their sex lives.
The episode is testament to the grip Serge Benhayon has on his followers, where dinner with an old friend can trigger a mandatory referral from your own wife.
A leaked membership list obtained by the Background Briefing podcast shows more than 900 people are signed up to the cult's online communications platform, many of them affluent and influential.
Despite a court finding Serge to be a "charlatan" leading a "sexually manipulative" and "socially harmful" cult, Universal Medicine has only grown in influence and wealth.

For the first time, a former longtime member has gone on the record to explain exclusively to the Background Briefing podcast how the cult has proved "unbreakable". It took Brendan about 20 years to escape Universal Medicine's grip. Now, he explains why.
The recruitment process
Brendan's recruitment began like many other disciples', in a massage parlour.
He was seeking relief for sore muscles from his intensive work as a tiler in south-west Sydney but got more than he bargained for.
The serenity was punctuated by the masseuse repeatedly burping, supposedly channelling the "bad energy" out of his body.
This was one of the bogus treatments pioneered by tennis coach-turned-guru Serge.
In 1999, at the age of 35, and having just emerged from bankruptcy with a wife and four children to support, Serge claimed to have a divine revelation on the toilet.
An ethereal voice supposedly told him all the knowledge in the universe was within his own body.
A high-school dropout with no formal training in science, medicine or religion, Serge devised a series of "esoteric" therapies that were essentially massage and acupuncture with a spiritual spiel.
He expanded from a clinic under his home in Goonellabah, northern New South Wales, to training up a network of practitioners and running group workshops.
Brendan's masseuse was one of these practitioners, and soon recommended a "heart chakra healing" course.
Having spurned his Catholic upbringing, Brendan was seeking a spiritual community and lifestyle and dabbled in eastern religion.
So, in 2006, he made the trip with his wife to the hippie hills of Byron Bay, where they first saw the "charismatic" Serge Benhayon on stage.

Gradually, the pair absorbed Serge's doctrine that there was an energetically "correct" version of everything, from the car you drove (ideally an Audi) to the music you played on your stereo (preferably produced by Serge's son).

Serge then gave his followers spiritual rankings, scoring himself above Jesus. "The drive and the competition went through the roof," Brendan says. The only way to ascend was to devote more time and money to Universal Medicine.
Any doubts Brendan had about the man claiming to be the reincarnation of luminaries including Leonardo Da Vinci were allayed by the calibre of Serge's followers.
"It covers up almost any red flags because you go, 'Well, I've got a surgeon over here, a doctor over here, a CEO over here, these people aren't silly,'" he says.

Serge loomed as a Messianic figure to his followers: in 2010, an acolyte named Rita Bone became the first in a series of cancer patients to leave almost everything to the cult, including her share of the house her surviving partner lived in.
Brendan says Serge's devotees came to believe he was the embodiment of a god.
"I believed the story, and if you really took it on, you would give your life over to it," he says. "You would defend it and you would die for it."
So, when Serge's first reckoning came in 2012, Brendan saw a call to arms.
Serge fosters a siege mentality

Business was booming when Serge was first exposed in the Australian media in 2012. He boasted 2,000 followers worldwide, a turnover of $2 million a year, and property worth almost $8 million, including Universal Medicine clinics in Brisbane and Lismore claiming to be "revolutionising healthcare".

Then, Professor John Dwyer, an eminent medical expert, publicly savaged Serge's treatments as bogus, and in some cases verging on sexual assault. He warned Serge's teachings could redirect acolytes from proper treatment for diseases such as cancer, which the cult leader always denied.
Most despicable to Professor Dwyer was the idea that "if you have any significant medical problems, it's your fault — you're being punished for sins in a previous life".
Australian media piled on, and one of those reporters was me.
Brendan first knows me as the 'antichrist'

I received a tip that Serge's cult had split more than 40 families, bringing me face to face with the leader himself, who looked more like a business coach than a guru in his buttoned-down collared shirt.

In a large conference room at Universal Medicine's expansive, leafy clinic site, I outed him as a bankrupt, a fact he at first denied, but then conceded ("Oh, '98, sorry"). He suggested that the partners of people who shunned their loved ones under his influence were to blame for the breakdown of their marriages.
I thought that Universal Medicine would fall apart under public scrutiny, but Brendan reveals how Serge manipulated the coverage to his own advantage.
When my story broke, Serge told the group I was "astral", which Brendan explains as the "antichrist" or "dark energy".
Brendan says the coverage made devotees defensive.
"They're calling us a cult, they're attacking us, we need to defend ourselves," he says of the group's mentality.
The cult launched a public relations counterattack, led by its many healthcare workers "to make Universal Medicine look legit, a healing organisation".
"We were asked to write in response to articles," Brendan recalls.
"There was a course on how to write about it, various websites … It was very organised and detailed."
The siege mentality saw Brendan move to Lismore in 2013 to be closer to the community, which was soon marshalled against a new enemy.
Serge deploys 'lawfare'

Serge stepped up the counter-offensive against a new foe: acupuncturist Esther Rockett, who was so disturbed by her massage session with the cult leader that she started a blog to expose Universal Medicine.
Esther believes she was hypnotised without consent, leading her to hyperventilate and convulse involuntarily, a technique she says she saw Serge replicate on 60 workshop attendees.
"I think that a lot of the people believed that they'd had a spiritual experience, and that's where he got them," Esther says.
Hypnotherapy could explain Serge's knack for converting specialist doctors who should be immune to pseudoscience, including one of Australia's leading paediatricians, Dr Howard Chilton.

When Esther named the health practitioners promoting the cult, they called for AHPRA to strip her acupuncture registration. Next, Serge asked a police officer to coach devotees on how to report Esther for "inciting violence" against Universal Medicine.
When that failed, Serge hit his bête noire with a defamation claim. A second suit from other cult members bankrupted Esther, leaving her couch surfing.
While Brendan feared the court case would bring more attention than Esther's blog itself, he didn't dare question Serge's judgement, even to his own wife.
Serge walked into the NSW Supreme Court in late 2018 wearing dark glasses, flanked by his immediate family who were all on the cult payroll.
"The whole family going together in lockstep, it's powerful" Brendan says.
"And you go, 'Hey, I'm part of that'."
But the show of strength was shaken by the opening question from top barrister, Tom Molomby, representing Esther on a no-win, no-fee basis.
"Mr Benhayon, in the time you've been in this courtroom… have there been any discarnate spirits in the room?"
As Serge floundered, Molomby made the case that the supposedly all-knowing guru was simply making up doctrine as he went.
He told the jury in closing that Serge was not crazy but "a crook".
"The person who sat opposite you in the witness box and lied his head off wasn't Pythagoras or Leonardo da Vinci," Molomby said. "It was Serge Benhayon, conman from Goonellabah."
"Not Mona Lisa anymore, huh? Mona liar."

The jury found all 38 of the imputations Esther had made about Serge to be true: that he was a "charlatan" who had an "indecent interest" in young girls, sexually manipulated followers, and swindled cancer patients.
This might have proven a fatal setback for others, but not Serge.
'Gaslighting' followers
Instead of owning his humiliating court loss, Serge "gaslit" his followers into thinking it was their fault for having "let the [evil] energy in", according to Brendan.
They responded by crowdfunding for his multimillion-dollar legal bill.
"I know people who put money in," Brendan says. "I don't know the full sum in the end but it was substantial."

The widely publicised court findings failed to stop new recruits, and Serge kept getting richer. The swindling of cancer patients escalated: the cult now runs webinars on how to hand over assets to the Benhayon family, coaching followers to clean cars and remove pilling from clothes prior to "passing over".
Serge sold his home near Lismore, on which he spent $1 million, to a billionaire's daughter, Jaye Scanlon, for $17 million, according to estate agents.

The following year, the cult announced Scanlon's ascension in its spiritual rankings, placing her just above Jesus Christ, according to a recording obtained by Background Briefing. Scanlon declined to answer questions.

Community backlash prompted Serge to relocate to a fresh locale where a multimillionaire swindler could better blend in — the Gold Coast — where his immediate family now owns $25 million in luxury property, including a waterfront mansion in the so-called "millionaire's playground" of Sovereign Island.
Serge more than survived the attack from cult outsiders, with his family now owning properties worth almost $50 million in NSW and Queensland alone.
The only cracks in the cult structure come from those within – and Serge has a plan for them too.
Shunning critics
Over time, Brendan saw up close what happens to followers who challenge Serge's ego.
One was Dr Howard Chilton, the top paediatric specialist whose daughter married Serge's son.
In 2018, the couple's 10 month-old infant was admitted to Lismore hospital in a critical condition with malnutrition from a Universal Medicine diet.

Dr Chilton helped ensure his grandson received proper treatment including being airlifted to Queensland Children's Hospital. This enraged the Benhayon family who considered it "hysteria" from the "irresponsible" Dr Chilton.

In a leaked email obtained by the Background Briefing podcast, Serge's wife claimed the baby was "detoxing from breastmilk" and Dr Chilton had been "channelling" dark energy by saying the cult diet "almost killed him".
The doctor's split from the group and resulting estrangement from his daughter reveals the cost of questioning Serge Benhayon, which Brendan himself would learn firsthand.
Dob in a detractor
After almost 20 years in Universal Medicine, Brendan Jones was kicked out "over a question", he says.

Late last year, Brendan saw a TV news story about a masseur charged with raping clients, someone he recognised as a Universal Medicine practitioner. Brendan asked Serge's son why the leader wasn't addressing the matter with the group.
Days later, Brendan was booted. In a leaked recording, Serge can be heard telling the cult faithful Brendan was a "detractor" who was "consciously evil".
Serge insulted Brendan regarding his job ("he just lays tiles") and the breakdown of his second marriage ("no coincidence he lost control of [his wife]").
The guru then warned followers that the enemies of Universal Medicine were "now close to you… a relationship, a love affair… a friend — next level treachery".

Serge urged followers to put their feelings about detractors into words, saying he had "commissioned" Brendan's ex-wives in the cult to write take-downs about him. "Brendan will be made famous," he said, adding, "Don't play threat with us."
Being shunned by the cult at the centre of his life left Brendan "beyond devastated" by the "brutalisation".
"I now have 1,200 people who will not communicate with me in any way," he says.
When he runs into former Universal Medicine friends taking his daughter to school, "I am the antichrist … and they will not even look at me", Brendan says.
Following his abrupt shunning, Brendan has rejoined the outside world, reconnecting with his sister, and even having his first beer in 18 years.
He's come to view Universal Medicine as "a complete scam".
"They're selling an afterlife and healing and making absolute multimillion-dollar wealth out of it, and there is no healing going on," he says.
But had Brendan not been kicked out of Universal Medicine, he says he would still be in it due to the brainwashing.
He wants Serge held to account, but can see the cult leader remains largely untouchable for regulators and police.
"Universal Medicine falls through the cracks, and that's how it's set up," Brendan says.
Professor Dwyer says his years of warning the public about the cult feel futile.
"There's no way to absolutely ban Benhayon and Universal Medicine," he says.
"All we can do is warn people … there are an awful lot of people who are very vulnerable to this sort of misinformation."
For both men, there's a glimmer of hope in a push to criminalise group coercion by cults, as recommended by a Victorian parliamentary inquiry.
To Brendan, Universal Medicine is a compelling example of why those laws should be fast-tracked.
"Because without the government agencies, you're on your own… financially, emotionally, mentally… it can cost you everything," he says.
The Unbreakable Cult is a six-part series from the Background Briefing podcast, available on ABC listen or wherever you get your podcasts.
